body:
hi -

contains_eager() does not imply any kind of WHERE or ON clause in a query, only additional columns to be fetched.  Therefore it has no interaction with the with_loader_criteria() feature.  docs are updated to clarify this. for additional criteria in your example, apply it within the select.join() method, e.g. `select(A).join(A.bs.and_(B.id == 1))`.    see https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/orm/queryguide.html#augmenting-built-in-on-clauses

I see this is for OSO.

This is expected behavior for now but I'd have to think about what the implications are for contains_eager() since it does indicate an entity load and perhaps would add a WHERE criteria as though someone had done `select(A, B)`.
unfortunately this wouldn't be possible to change for 1.4 as it's not backwards compatible.

rename.from: with_loader_criteria does not apply criteria with contains_eager
rename.to: consider with_loader_criteria adding WHERE criteria for a contains_eager() ?

body:
given

```py
class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String)
    bs = relationship("B")


class B(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'b'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    a_id = Column(ForeignKey("a.id"))
    data = Column(String)
```

these queries apply the criteria even if B is not selected:

```
print(
    s.query(A, B).join(A.bs).options(with_loader_criteria(B, B.data == 'x1')).all()
)

print(
    s.query(A).join(A.bs).options(with_loader_criteria(B, B.data == 'x1')).all()
)

```

these dont work:

```
print(
    s.query(A, B).join(B).options(with_loader_criteria(B, B.data == 'x1')).all()
)

print(
    s.query(A).join(B).options(with_loader_criteria(B, B.data == 'x1')).all()
)
```

that's a bug.  this is the fix:

```diff
diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py
index 8e0fd44cda..f36f1900dc 100644
--- a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py
+++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py
@@ -1647,8 +1647,12 @@ class _ORMJoin(expression.Join):
 
             self._target_adapter = target_adapter
 
+        augment_onclause = onclause is None and _extra_criteria
         expression.Join.__init__(self, left, right, onclause, isouter, full)
 
+        if augment_onclause:
+            self.onclause &= sql.and_(*_extra_criteria)
+
         if (
             not prop
             and getattr(right_info, "mapper", None)

```


however for the example you have here:

```
    subquery = select(A).join(B).subquery(name='sub')
    subquery_aliased = aliased(A, alias=subquery, flat=True, adapt_on_names=True)
    query = select(subquery_aliased).options(
        contains_eager(subquery_aliased.bs, alias=subquery),
        with_loader_criteria(B, B.id == 1, include_aliases=True),
    )
```

there's no B entity there, that query is going through extra effort to enclose the JOIN to B and I dont see how that one can work.

body:
re: the subquery, the problem is WLC works in one of two ways; it adds a WHERE clause to entities that are in the query which are themselves in the FROM list as a non-join target, or if the entitiy is in the FROM list as a join target, then it adds criteria to the ON clause.   What we can't do is add a WHERE clause to entities that are in the FROM list as join targets, because that breaks OUTER JOIN.

so in this example we can't control that "subquery" doesnt OUTER JOIN to B, in which case we can't generically add limiting criteria to it, such as "B.security_group = 'foo'" because that will eliminate any A rows that don't have a B.

this is the fundamental reason WLC can augment something like joinedload(), because we wrote the ON clause, but can't easily augment contains_eager(), since it would have to guess where it's supposed to modify the query. in that subquery example, it's extra hard to figure out.

I know OSOs use case but I dont know what the solution to that would be, other than either warning for that use case, or filtering at the result level but that is not efficient.

so I will do the select(A).join(B) use case, i can do that now, and clarify the docs some more.   the subquery thing I don't have a solution for that right now other than documenting it but i will revisit if i think of something.

the subquery doesnt even render correctly in any case, so i dont think this is even a real use case, note the extra "b" and the cartesian product.   I tried a few varieties without success:

```sql
SELECT b.id, b.a_id, b.data, b.flag, anon_1.id AS id_1, anon_1.data AS data_1 
FROM b, (SELECT a.id AS id, a.data AS data 
FROM a LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id AND b.id = :id_2) AS anon_1
```

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**fix with_loader_criteria for select(A).join(B)** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3168
